messages.subject: General questions about filtering/normalizing CpG counts
messages.subject_clean: General questions about filtering/normalizing CpG counts
messages.body_plain:
Hi Altuna,

thanks for creating (and maintaining!) methylKit!

I am fairly new to WGBS and RRBS analysis, and I'm trying to understand the impact of filterByCoverage() and normalizeCoverage(). I totally understand that bins with extreme read coverages may represent PCR artifacts, so filterByCoverage makes sense, but why do you need to normalize for coverage differences? After all, you are going to compare fractions of methylated Cs anyway, so the coverage, presumably, won't play a role there anymore.
One thing I can envision is that extreme differences in sequencing depth between different conditions may lead to an increase of false positive DMRs (i.e., if regions are not sufficiently covered in one condition, but the other). Do you have any insights into when the normalizeCoverage() function should be used, i.e. any QC that you do in order to establish whether it's needed or not?

My second question is: do you recommend filtering and/or normalizing the read counts before or after summarizing them per genomic tiles or regions?

Best,

Friederike

messages.subject_clean: [methylkit_discussion] General questions about filtering/normalizing CpG counts
messages.body_plain:
Hi Friederike,

>
>
>
> I am fairly new to WGBS and RRBS analysis, and I'm trying to understand the impact of filterByCoverage() and normalizeCoverage(). I totally understand that bins with extreme read coverages may represent PCR artifacts, so filterByCoverage makes sense, but why do you need to normalize for coverage differences? After all, you are going to compare fractions of methylated Cs anyway, so the coverage, presumably, won't play a role there anymore.

Test results are associated with coverage, if you keep the ratios same but change coverage p-values will change, you can easily test that with Fisher's exact test.

> One thing I can envision is that extreme differences in sequencing depth between different conditions may lead to an increase of false positive DMRs (i.e., if regions are not sufficiently covered in one condition, but the other). Do you have any insights into when the normalizeCoverage() function should be used, i.e. any QC that you do in order to establish whether it's needed or not?

I think filtering  should be used in RRBS, normalization can be used if sequencing depth between two samples are very different. You can look at the coverage distributions to gauge that but I don't have a rule of thumb, many people just ignore this issue. For WGBS, you can remove duplicate reads that will help with PCR bias, so filtering may not be necessary.

>
> My second question is: do you recommend filtering and/or normalizing the read counts before or after summarizing them per genomic tiles or regions?

I think filtering should be done before summarizing, I'm not so sure about normalization. the order probably doesn't matter. You can make an experiment and update this post.

Best,
Altuna

messages.subject: SVA for batch effect correction
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I'm not sure how you can use the sva package for correcting batch effects. I have a dataset of 15 samples and there seems to be batch effects due to the samples run on different days. In PCA clustering the samples tend to cluster according to the batch rather than treatment. Can mr. Akalin or someone else give some exmaple code on how to do this? I'm not an expert in R. Here's my code, it's almost the same as the example code in the documentation.

#Example analysis
#Read methylation files

library(methylKit)

# this is a list of example files, ships with the package
# for your own analysis you will just need to provide set of paths to files
# you will not need the "system.file(..."  part
file.list=list( "/media/jsalmi/storage1/mimi_rrbs/sams/merged_1.sorted.sam",
                "/media/jsalmi/storage1/mimi_rrbs/sams/merged_6.sorted.sam",
                "/media/jsalmi/storage1/mimi_rrbs/sams/merged_11.sorted.sam",
                "/media/jsalmi/storage1/mimi_rrbs/sams/merged_3.sorted.sam",
                "/media/jsalmi/storage1/mimi_rrbs/sams/merged_8.sorted.sam",
                "/media/jsalmi/storage1/mimi_rrbs/sams/merged_13.sorted.sam")

# read the files to a methylRawList object: myobj
myobj=read.bismark( file.list,
            sample.id <http://sample.id>=list("1","6","11","3","8","13"),
                           assembly="hg19",treatment=c(0,0,0,1,1,1))

#Get descriptive stats on methylation

# get methylation statistics on second file "test2" in myobj which is a class of methylRawList
getMethylationStats(myobj[[2]],plot=F,both.strands=F)

# plot methylation statistics on second file "test2" in myobj which is a class of methylRawList
getMethylationStats(myobj[[2]],plot=T,both.strands=F)

#Get bases covered by all samples and cluster samples

# see what the data looks like for sample 2 in myobj methylRawList
head(myobj[[2]])

# merge all samples to one table by using base-pair locations that are covered in all samples
# setting destrand=TRUE, will merge reads on both strans of a CpG dinucleotide. This provides better
# coverage, but only advised when looking at CpG methylation
meth=unite(myobj,destrand=TRUE)

# merge all samples to one table by using base-pair locations that are covered in all samples
#
meth=unite(myobj)

# cluster all samples using correlation distance and return a tree object for plclust
hc = clusterSamples(meth, dist="correlation", method="ward", plot=FALSE)

# cluster all samples using correlation distance and plot hiarachical clustering
clusterSamples(meth, dist="correlation", method="ward", plot=TRUE)

# screeplot of principal component analysis.
PCASamples(meth, screeplot=TRUE)

# principal component anlaysis of all samples.
PCASamples(meth)

#Calculate differential methylation

#Before differential methylation calculation, consider filtering high coverage bases to remove potential PCR bias using filterByCoverage(). In addition, consider normalizing read coverages between samples to avoid bias introduced by systematically more sequenced samples, using normalizeCoverage().

# calculate differential methylation p-values and q-values
myDiff=calculateDiffMeth(meth, num.cores=2)

# check how data part of methylDiff object looks like
head( myDiff )

# get differentially methylated regions with 10% difference and qvalue<0.05
myDiff10p=get.methylDiff(myDiff,difference=10,qvalue=0.1)

# get differentially hypo methylated regions with 10% difference and qvalue<0.05
myDiff10pHypo =get.methylDiff(myDiff,difference=10,qvalue=0.1,type="hypo")

# get differentially hyper methylated regions with 10% difference and qvalue<0.05
myDiff10pHyper=get.methylDiff(myDiff,difference=10,qvalue=0.1,type="hyper")

#Annotate differentially methylated bases/regions

# read-in transcript locations to be used in annotation
# IMPORTANT: annotation files that come with the package (version >=0.5) are a subset of full annotation
# files. Download appropriate annotation files from UCSC (or other sources) in BED format
gene.obj=read.transcript.features("/media/jsalmi/storage1/mimi_rrbs/GRCh38.bed")

# annotate differentially methylated Cs with promoter/exon/intron using annotation data
#annotate.WithGenicParts(myDiff10p,gene.obj)

#get the distance to TSS and nearest gene name
diffAnn <-annotate.WithGenicParts(myDiff10p, gene.obj)

#target.row is the row number in myDiff25p
head(getAssociationWithTSS(diffAnn))

# get percentage/number of differentially methylated regions that overlap with intron/exon/promoters
getTargetAnnotationStats(diffAnn,percentage=TRUE, precedence=TRUE)

#We can also plot the percentage of differentially methylated bases overlapping with exon/intron/promoters
plotTargetAnnotation(diffAnn, precedence=TRUE, main="differential methylation annotation")

cpg.obj <- read.feature.flank("/media/jsalmi/storage1/mimi_rrbs/GRCh38.bed",feature.flank.name <http://feature.flank.name> = c("CpGi", "shores"))
diffCpGann <- annotate.WithFeature.Flank(myDiff10p, cpg.obj$CpGi,cpg.obj$shores, feature.name <http://feature.name>= "CpGi", flank.name <http://flank.name>="shores")

plotTargetAnnotation(diffCpGann,col =c("green", "gray", "white"), main="differential methylation annotation")

getFeatsWithTargetsStats(diffAnn, percentage =TRUE)

genelist10<-getAssociationWithTSS(diffAnn)
write.table(genelist10, file="/home/jsalmi/genelist10_test1")

messages.body_plain:
Webinar: Forecasting With Predictive Analytics and Data Science

Registration: http://hubs.ly/H019XtK0
*Alternative link: http://info.salford-systems.com/forecasting-webinar

September 22, 10AM – 11AM PDT
* If the time is inconvenient, please register and we will send you a recording.

Abstract:   Forecasting with predictive analytics offers the opportunity to leverage the huge amounts of data, now readily available, that exhibit the following characteristics:
·         Data that changes over time, as well as static data
·         Perhaps hundreds, thousands of independent variables
·         Data reflective of today’s ever-changing economic environment

With data mining and machine learning methods, your data can easily and quickly be converted into knowledge to yield more accurate and more actionable models. We will demonstrate these techniques on a data set from a Brazilian grocery store chain. Information including date, store, promotions, climate, and unit price will be used to predict the total sales of oranges for the company. The model will help you identify what affects sales, decide on best prices and promos, and most importantly, forecast sales in the future.

 Additionally, we will go beyond the retail industry and touch on:

                Case Studies:
                                •Forecasting Alaska’s Ecosystem in the 22nd Century
                                •Atmospheric Pollution Forecasting
                                •Forecasting Recessions with MARS

Although we show 4 examples, the approach is widely applicable and you will be able to follow the same steps on your own datasets. Examples of datasets that would benefit include:
·         Business: Marketing forecasts, targeted sales forecasts, fraud detection
·         Drug Discovery: forecasting the onset of disease, forecasting healthcare outcomes
·         Insurance: forecasting response to a premium change, forecasting costs at the onset of a claim
·         Environmental: decision making for environmental management, population dynamics, habitat suitability, forecast weather conditions throughout
                                  the world
·         Epidemiology: risk analysis, population dynamics

This webinar will be a step-by-step presentation that you can repeat on your own!
Included with Registration:
·         Webinar recording
·         30 day software evaluation
·         Dataset used in presentation
·         Step-by-step instruction for you to try at home

Who should attend:
·         Attend if you want to implement data science techniques even without a data science, statistical or programming background.
·         Attend if you want to understand why data science techniques are so important for forecasting.

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] SVA for batch effect correction
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I don't have an example code for that. But we have all the functionality for re-creating a methylBase object after unwanted variation is removed from the percent methylation matrix. Please update us if you get to using SVA or something similar.

A crude way of dealing with this is to remove PC that matches the batch effect. you can use assocComp() and removeComp() functions for those tasks.

Best,
Altuna
